KEY MESSAGE 1...A stationary front draped across the Southern 
Appalachians is forecast to lift slowly north and east through 
tonight in advance of a shortwave dropping southeast out of the 
Great Lakes. Modest moisture and instability along the 
boundary, plus enhanced convergence near a weak surface low 
traversing the boundary, appears sufficient for a convective 
cluster to develop along the higher terrain and drop southeast 
from central VA into northeast NC later today and tonight. 
Convective, global, and ensemble guidance have shown a 
consistently strong signal for this convective cluster despite 
only modest instability and moisture. That said, guidance is 
also in pretty good agreement depicting a weakening trend with 
the convection as it approaches ENC. Right now, it appears the 
greatest chance of seeing thunderstorms overnight will be from 
Lenoir County north through Martin County. The risk of severe 
weather appears low, but the environment appears supportive of 
some small hail or gusty winds in the strongest cores.

On Monday, daytime heating of the airmass in the vicinity of 
the seabreeze and any residual boundaries from tonight's 
convection should support a renewed risk of thunderstorms. Once 
again, some of these could be strong to marginally severe. 
Residually dry air aloft should support DCAPE values of 1000+ 
j/kg. This in tandem with steep low-level lapse rates and 
moderate instability should lead to the primary risk being 
damaging winds of 40-65 mph. Forecast aids like the ECMWF's EFI 
show a decent environmental signal for a few severe 
thunderstorms which is also supported by short-range ensemble 
guidance. The convective potential on Monday should primarily be
diurnally-driven, with the risk decreasing after sunset Monday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...An anomalously strong upper level trough is 
forecast to develop over the Mid-Atlantic Region on Tuesday, 
with a potent shortwave diving southeast through Virginia and 
the Carolinas Tuesday into Tuesday night. A strong LLJ ahead of 
this feature should lead to increasing moisture advection, with 
PWATs once again climbing back above 2". Meanwhile, heating of a
moist boundary layer should support moderate instability, with 
MLCAPE rising into the 1000-1500j/kg range. Aloft, a notable 
upper jet max is forecast to overspread the instability axis, 
supporting deep layer shear of 30- 45kt. While instability will 
be moderate, the shear/instability combo is notable for this 
time of year, as is the amount of lift expected. 

Synoptically, the combination of all of the factors above 
checks a lot of boxes for severe weather potential. This also 
has overwhelming support from ensemble, analog, and machine 
learning guidance. The main potential limiting factor is timing.
Recent guidance suggests convection may not reach ENC until 
after sunset. Despite the potential for a gradually stabilizing 
boundary layer, the strong large-scale forcing should help 
support deep convection well past the typical diurnal max in 
convective intensity this time of year. Given the amount of 
forcing present, it appears likely that an MCS will move through
ENC during the evening and early overnight hours posing a risk 
of damaging winds. Low-level SRH around 100m2/s2 may support a 
few rotating updrafts capable of hail and perhaps a brief 
tornado. However, those latter 2 hazards should be lower 
compared to the wind risk. Lastly, while a MCS would be more 
progressive, the high PWAT airmass should support heavy rainfall
rates which may support a short-fused flooding risk, especially
for the area hardest hit the past few days (ie. Hyde County 
east through the Outer Banks).

Ahead of the convection, hot and humid conditions are expected,
with heat indices rising to 100-105 degrees. This appears to be
a bit marginal for heat headlines, but is something we'll 
continue to assess in later forecasts.
